body.text: Shenzhen may not produce a new Yalta, nor is there much reason to expect a breakthrough in nuclear arms control or the resolution of regional conflicts. But the image of Trump, Xi and Putin sitting together will carry its own geopolitical significance

The proposed meeting between US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the APEC Economic Leaders’ Meeting in Shenzhen on November 18-19, 2026, could prove to be one of the more consequential diplomatic spectacles of the year.

The gathering would mark the first-ever joint engagement between the leaders of the world's three largest nuclear powers. Expected towards the conclusion of Trump's China visit, the meeting is significant not so much for the agreements it might produce as for the geopolitical message it seeks to convey.

Indeed, expectations of substantive outcomes remain deliberately modest. American officials have characterised the encounter as an entry point for dialogue rather than a negotiating forum for formal agreements. Yet, in contemporary geopolitics, symbolism is rarely inconsequential. The very fact that Washington, Beijing and Moscow are willing to share a diplomatic platform at the highest political level reflects a recognition that the management of global instability increasingly requires direct engagement among the principal centres of power.
The motivations of the three leaders, however, are far from identical.

For Trump, the central imperative is to establish a framework for nuclear arms control that reflects the changing distribution of global power. The expiry of the New START treaty in February 2026 has brought an end to the last formal limitations on the strategic nuclear arsenals of the United States and Russia. Washington is consequently seeking a more expansive arrangement that incorporates China.

Trump's ambition to bring Beijing to the negotiating table reflects a broader American concern that the existing architecture of nuclear arms control is increasingly disconnected from contemporary strategic realities. China, with an estimated 600 nuclear warheads compared with more than 5,000 each in the American and Russian arsenals, remains reluctant to accept constraints designed around a fundamentally different strategic balance. The ongoing conflict involving Iran adds another layer of urgency to Washington's diplomatic calculations. Significantly, Ukraine is being kept outside the trilateral framework, with American officials insisting that the conflict must be addressed through a separate negotiating track.

For Putin, the proposed encounter represents an opportunity to reclaim diplomatic relevance. Moscow has reportedly been an important advocate of the trilateral format, with Putin raising the possibility during an October 2026 conversation with Trump. Russia's interest is not confined to the immediate question of nuclear arms control.

It is also about restoring its position as an indispensable interlocutor in the management of international security. After years of Western isolation following its invasion of Ukraine, a seat alongside the American and Chinese presidents would itself constitute a considerable diplomatic achievement. The Kremlin would naturally prefer to use such an occasion to advance discussions on Ukraine. Washington, however, appears unwilling to allow Moscow to turn the trilateral engagement into a forum for legitimising its territorial and strategic claims.

Xi Jinping's calculations are somewhat different. Hosting the meeting provides Beijing with an opportunity to consolidate its image as a central actor in global diplomacy. Shenzhen, the embodiment of China's extraordinary economic and technological transformation, offers an especially appropriate setting for such a projection of power. For Xi, the encounter also provides an opportunity to manage an increasingly consequential relationship with Washington at a time when the fragile trade truce between the two countries is approaching its January 2027 expiry.

Beijing can demonstrate diplomatic flexibility without necessarily accepting binding commitments on nuclear arms control or Ukraine. China's relative caution in public messaging is indicative of this preference: it is willing to facilitate great-power engagement, but not at the cost of compromising its strategic interests.

The meeting also reflects Trump's preference for personalised, leader-driven diplomacy. His approach rests on the proposition that geopolitical problems can be addressed through direct political engagement among powerful leaders, often bypassing the institutional constraints and diplomatic processes that traditionally govern international negotiations. This approach may generate openings that conventional diplomacy struggles to create. But it also raises questions about the durability of any understandings reached through such personalised engagements, particularly when the underlying strategic interests of the participants remain deeply divergent.

The international significance of the proposed Shenzhen meeting extends well beyond its immediate agenda. Comparisons with the 1945 Yalta Conference are inevitable, though somewhat premature. Unlike Yalta, this gathering is not about negotiating a comprehensive division of the international order. Yet, the optics are consequential: they reinforce the emergence of a more explicitly multipolar world in which the principal powers increasingly seek to manage global security through direct bargaining.

The willingness of Washington, Beijing and Moscow to engage collectively underscores their shared claim to a privileged position in the international system, reinforcing the perception, particularly across the Global South, that power politics and transactional diplomacy are increasingly displacing the normative foundations of the liberal international order.

For Xi Jinping, hosting the meeting offers an opportunity to project China as an indispensable diplomatic actor and an equal interlocutor of the United States. For Vladimir Putin, sharing the platform with Trump and Xi would represent a significant diplomatic rehabilitation after years of Western isolation, reinforcing Moscow's claim that Russia remains too consequential to be excluded from global power calculations.

The implications, however, are less reassuring for American allies and partners. Ukraine and European capitals will be concerned about the prospect of their security interests being negotiated over their heads, while Asian partners such as Japan, South Korea, Australia and the Philippines may question the durability of American commitments if Washington appears increasingly invested in direct accommodation with Beijing and Moscow. Such perceptions could encourage greater hedging and strategic autonomy among US partners.

More fundamentally, the meeting raises questions about the future of multilateral institutions and the normative foundations of the international order. Supporters would regard direct engagement among major powers as pragmatic realism in an increasingly interdependent world, where nuclear risks, technological competition and regional conflicts demand sustained dialogue.

Critics, however, would caution that great-power bargains risk legitimising coercion, weakening deterrence and accelerating a return to spheres of influence. For smaller states, the danger is that their strategic interests become subordinate to the calculations of a select group of powerful actors. Ultimately, Shenzhen may not produce a new Yalta, but it could reinforce a defining feature of contemporary geopolitics: an emerging international order in which great-power accommodation and competition increasingly take precedence over multilateral consensus and established norms.

For India, the proposed encounter merits particular attention. New Delhi has consistently sought to preserve strategic autonomy while maintaining consequential relationships with all three powers. A world in which Washington, Beijing and Moscow increasingly privilege direct bilateral and trilateral bargains could create both opportunities and constraints for Indian diplomacy. India would welcome any serious effort to stabilise nuclear competition and reduce the risks of major-power confrontation. At the same time, it would be wary of arrangements that institutionalise a privileged great-power directorate or diminish the agency of other significant actors.

The central challenge for Indian diplomacy will be to ensure that the emergence of a more transactional international order does not translate into a system in which the interests of countries outside the inner circle of major powers become expendable.

India's own engagement with the United States, Russia and China demonstrates the importance of maintaining diplomatic flexibility in an increasingly fragmented strategic environment. The Shenzhen meeting will therefore be an important indicator of how the major powers intend to manage their competition and whether their emerging diplomatic arrangements will accommodate the interests of other consequential states.

Ultimately, the significance of the Trump-Xi-Putin encounter may lie less in what the three leaders agree upon than in what their meeting reveals about the changing character of international politics. The post-Cold War assumption that global stability would be sustained through American primacy, multilateral institutions and a broadly shared normative framework is increasingly difficult to reconcile with ontemporary geopolitical realities. What is emerging instead is a more fluid and contested order in which major powers are simultaneously competing for influence and exploring mechanisms to manage their mutual vulnerabilities.

Shenzhen may not produce a new Yalta, nor is there much reason to expect a breakthrough in nuclear arms control or the resolution of regional conflicts. But the image of Trump, Xi and Putin sitting together will carry its own geopolitical significance. It will suggest that, even in an era of intensifying strategic rivalry, the principal nuclear powers continue to regard one another as the indispensable interlocutors in the management of global order. The larger question is whether this renewed great-power diplomacy can produce a measure of stability or whether it will accelerate the emergence of an international system in which the interests of the powerful increasingly take precedence over the principles that have traditionally underpinned the global order.
This commentary originally appeared in Moneycontrol.
